# When the Drawing Rests: How Conservation Rotations Alter a Gallery’s Story

## Summary

The Veyra Museum of Civic Arts rotates light-sensitive works in its permanent gallery *Street and Studio, 1880–1935* after fixed exposure limits. Although these changes originate in conservation policy, each replacement also changes the sequence through which visitors encounter the gallery’s themes. This analysis asks whether replacement works preserve both visitor attention and the curatorial role of the objects they replace.

Across 14 rotations observed over 18 months, replacement works had a 4.7 percentage-point lower stop rate than the outgoing works. That average conceals a more useful pattern: replacements judged to have strong narrative continuity performed similarly to their predecessors, while low-continuity replacements lost 11.7 percentage points. Dwell time among visitors who did stop changed little. The principal effect was therefore on whether an object attracted attention at all, not on how long it held attention once selected.

The results support treating conservation rotations as small acts of re-curation rather than as technically equivalent substitutions. They do not establish that narrative continuity caused the observed differences, because object size, season, familiarity, and gallery programming were not fully controlled.

## Gallery and dataset

The gallery contains 28 objects arranged in four sections: labor, movement, private interiors, and public design. Nine positions are reserved for drawings, watercolors, or prints that require periodic rest. A rotation normally keeps the mount, case, and neighboring objects unchanged, but the incoming work may differ in medium, dimensions, subject, or interpretive purpose.

The museum combined four internal data sources:

- anonymous ceiling-sensor counts for 18,742 gallery entries;
- zone-level dwell records sampled at ten-second intervals;
- 14 rotation logs covering six display positions;
- label and object records used to assess continuity between outgoing and incoming works.

For each rotation, the comparison used the final two weeks of the outgoing display and days 3–16 of the replacement display. Weekdays and opening hours were matched. School-group periods, evening events, installation days, and intervals with sensor outages were excluded. The matched sample contained 12,125 visitor routes.

A “stop” meant remaining in an object’s zone for at least eight seconds. “Route completion” meant reaching the gallery’s final section after entering the first. These measures describe movement rather than comprehension.

## Measuring continuity

Three museum curators independently scored each replacement pair from 1 to 5. They used object records and label text but were not shown visitor data. A score of 5 indicated that the replacement served the same function in the gallery argument—for example, another image of mechanized street movement from a similar period. A score of 1 indicated that it occupied the same physical position but introduced a substantially different subject or interpretive role.

The reviewers’ weighted agreement was moderate (kappa = 0.58). Their mean scores produced three groups:

- **high continuity (4–5):** 6 rotations;
- **medium continuity (3):** 5 rotations;
- **low continuity (1–2):** 3 rotations.

This index captures institutional judgments about the gallery’s intended story. It should not be read as an objective measure of what every visitor perceived.

## Results

| Rotation group | Number of rotations | Outgoing stop rate | Replacement stop rate | Difference |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| All rotations | 14 | 41.8% | 37.1% | -4.7 pp |
| High continuity | 6 | 42.2% | 41.6% | -0.6 pp |
| Medium continuity | 5 | 40.7% | 37.0% | -3.7 pp |
| Low continuity | 3 | 43.1% | 31.4% | -11.7 pp |

An event-cluster bootstrap placed the overall stop-rate difference between -8.3 and -1.2 percentage points. Estimates within the three continuity groups are less stable because each group contains few rotations, especially the low-continuity category.

Median dwell among visitors who stopped was 27.4 seconds for outgoing works and 26.9 seconds for replacements. The half-second difference was small relative to variation among objects. Route completion fell from 63.5% to 60.8% overall. Most of that decline occurred during low-continuity rotations, where completion dropped by 8.9 percentage points.

One high-continuity pair illustrates the pattern. A charcoal drawing of commuters beneath the fictional Marris Viaduct was replaced by a watercolor of passengers boarding the North Quay tram. The works differed in medium and palette, but both linked the labor section to the following section on urban movement. Stop rates were 44.0% and 43.6%, respectively.

By contrast, a crowded print of a garment workshop was replaced by a geometric municipal bathhouse plan because the two sheets fit the same mat and exposure schedule. The replacement was visually precise and historically relevant, but it weakened the transition from domestic sewing to factory labor. Its stop rate was 13 percentage points lower, and fewer visitors continued to the next labor display.

## Other factors

An exploratory model included continuity score, visible image area, tonal contrast with the wall, label length, and gallery attendance. Each one-point increase in continuity was associated with a 2.6 percentage-point increase in stop rate after adjustment. Larger image area also had a positive association. Label length and daily attendance had little apparent relationship with stopping.

This model is descriptive. Fourteen rotation events provide a thin basis for estimating several related influences, and tonal contrast was coded by one collections technician rather than measured instrumentally. The coefficients should therefore be treated as prompts for future testing, not as stable predictions.

Eight replacements carried a short label sentence explaining why the preceding work was resting. These displays generated 3.8 object-page scans per 100 visitors, compared with 2.1 for replacements without such a sentence. The labels were not assigned randomly: curators tended to add explanations to more prominent or complicated rotations. The scan difference cannot be attributed to the explanation alone.

## Implications for curatorial practice

The clearest operational lesson is that matching dimensions and exposure limits is insufficient. Before approving a rotation, the museum could score candidates against three questions: Does the incoming work perform the same role in the section? Does it preserve the transition to neighboring objects? Does its scale remain legible from the established visitor path? A candidate weak on two of these questions may require changes to adjacent labels or object order.

The museum should also retain brief rotation explanations, but test them systematically. Alternating explanatory and standard labels across comparable rotations would reveal whether transparency increases engagement or merely attracts visitors already interested in conservation.

Finally, future analysis should use a contemporaneous comparison zone elsewhere in the museum and treat each rotation—not each visitor—as the main unit of inference. Repeat visitors were not identified, visitor characteristics were not collected, and sensor stops cannot show whether people understood the intended narrative. Even with those limits, the observed pattern suggests that conservation-driven substitutions can preserve attention when they also preserve curatorial function.
